issues.issue: The cross-reference is to "Section XDI" (Section XIII), and the clause fixes a termination date of 05/13/2009 that does not match Item 2 of the original Declarations (04/13/2009). Which document fixes the true termination date, and hence when the Discovery Period begins, is open to construction.

The Discovery Period table sets a $160,000 retention for Directors and Officers Liability, which matches neither the $0 retention for Insuring Agreement (A) nor the $100,000 retention for Insuring Agreement (B) in Item 9 of the Declarations. Which retention governs a Discovery Period claim cannot be resolved from the two documents together.

"The acquiring entity" is not a defined term and "Financial Impairment" is defined in Section IV (I) only as a status of the Company, so the clause's exception is measured by a definition that on its face cannot apply to an acquirer. Whether the Insuring Agreement (B) retention attaches when the acquirer simply declines to indemnify is left open.

"The acquiring entity" is added to the definition of Company without being defined or identified anywhere in the Policy, and no test (asset purchase, merger, receivership sale) is given for who qualifies. The double limitation "only for Wrongful Acts involving the entity or entities set forth in Item 1" and "only for Wrongful Acts occurring prior to the termination date" further leaves the acquirer's status uncertain.

By making the acquiring entity part of the "Company," this amendment feeds directly into the Insured vs. Insured Exclusion in Section V (J), which bars Claims brought by or on behalf of the Company. Whether a suit by the acquirer or by a receiver standing in its place is thereby excluded is a conflict between this definition and Section V (J).

This states the Discovery Period premium is fully earned, while Section XIII (B)(2) obliges the Insurer to return 100% of unearned premium on Insurer cancellation. The two cannot both operate if the Insurer terminates coverage during the Discovery Period.

The Endorsement takes effect at 12:01 a.m. on 05/13/2009, the identical moment at which paragraph 1 of the same Endorsement terminates the Policy. Whether the Discovery Period begins before, at, or after termination is a question the two dates leave open.

This says nothing herein varies the Policy's terms, yet the same Endorsement deletes Section XII in its entirety and replaces the Section IV (E) definition of Company. The reach of the "other than as above stated" qualifier against those deletions is open to construction.

The notice states Defense Costs are included within the Limit of Liability, but Section XVI (K) says headings and descriptions form no part of the terms of coverage and this notice is not an operative provision. Whether the notice can be relied on as a term, alongside Section IX (A)(1), is arguable.

The Named Insured entry is garbled and partly illegible ("vant ederal Sa ares, Inc."), so the identity and order of the listed insured entities cannot be read off the face of the Declarations. Since Section IV (P) defines "Named Insured" as the first entity in Item 1, the defect matters.

The expiration date is printed as "0443/2009" and is superseded by the Amendment to Declarations extending the Policy Period to 05/13/2009. Which date governs "Policy Period" under Section IV (R) is not resolvable from Item 2 alone.

The $10,000,000 Total Policy Limit for all Insuring Agreements is stated against Item 8 limits that separately total $35,000,000, and Section VII (A)(1) and (A)(2) treat those limits differently. How the aggregate cap interacts with the individual limits is left to construction.

"If the eligibility requirements are met" identifies no requirements and points to no section, leaving the conditions for exercising the Discovery Period undefined in the Declarations. Section III supplies conditions but this Item does not incorporate them by reference.

Coverage is conditioned on a "Limit of Liability, retention and premium" being set forth, but Insuring Agreement (A) shows a retention of "N/A"/$0 and Agreements (A) and (B) share a single row. Whether the prerequisite is satisfied for Insuring Agreement (A) is arguable against Section I.

This says Insuring Agreement (C) includes Securities Liability coverage, yet Endorsement 2949 adds a Securities Liability Exclusion to Section V and a separate Securities Liability Insuring Agreement (Form 5098) is issued. Whether securities claims fall under (C) or exclusively under the endorsement is a conflict between this note and those endorsements.

The Item fixes a $5,000 IRA/Keogh retention but then says that if IRA/Keogh coverage is provided by Endorsement the retention shall be that "set forth in Item 9," giving two different retentions for the same class of Claim. The cross-reference is also miscited as "Section ITV (X)(2)."

The list of incorporated Endorsements ends in illegible characters ("500! | 5 0€ > aH"), so which forms are incorporated cannot be determined from the text. The later Declarations amendments list a different set of forms (5081, 5082).

This makes the Declarations, Application, Policy and Endorsements the contract, while Section XVI (B) states that the Policy, Application and written Endorsements "constitute the entire agreement" without mentioning the Declarations. The two integration statements are not identical in scope.

This extends the Policy Period to 05/13/2009 while Item 2 of the original Declarations and the definitions of Policy Period and Policy Year in Section IV (R) and (S) key off the original 04/13/2009 expiration. Whether the extra month is a new Policy Year or part of the last one is a question the two provisions leave unresolved.

This Endorsement schedule (5081, 5082, 2223, 2949, 5091, 5093, 5098, TRIA-01, 8790D) differs from the schedules in Item 13 of the original Declarations and of the 2007 amendment. Which schedule identifies the forms actually incorporated is open to dispute.
The clause says nothing varies the Policy while the same Endorsement changes the Policy Period in Item 2. The scope of "other than as above stated" is the point of construction.

Vantus Bank is inserted as the first entity listed, which changes who the "Named Insured" is under Section IV (P) and therefore who may cancel, receive notice and act for all Insureds under Sections XIII (A) and XVI (D). Nothing in the Endorsement addresses that consequence.

This schedule omits form 5082 (the later Policy Period amendment) and differs from the schedules in the other two Item 13 provisions. Which endorsements are incorporated at which date is unresolved between them.
The preservation sentence sits in an Endorsement that in fact changes the Named Insured in Item 1. What "other than as above stated" preserves is arguable.

Coverage is withheld unless a Limit of Liability, retention AND premium are "set forth in the Declarations," but Item 6/9 show "$0" or "N/A" retention for Insuring Agreement (A) and no separate premium for Agreement (B). Whether those Agreements satisfy the tri-partite condition is a conflict with the Declarations table.

The carve-out "except for Loss the Company pays as indemnification" does not say what happens where the Company is legally permitted but unable to indemnify, a gap Section VII (B)(1) addresses differently. The phrase's boundary is the point of construction.

"Has agreed to or is legally permitted or required by law to indemnify" gives coverage on a permissive-indemnification basis without saying whether actual payment is required. Section VII (B)(2) treats permitted-but-unpaid indemnification as within Insuring Agreement (B), which sharpens the ambiguity.

This grant of Company liability coverage is cut back by the Securities Liability Exclusion added to Section V by Endorsement 2949, while Item 6 of the Declarations states that Insuring Agreement (C) includes Securities Liability coverage. The two cannot both be given effect.

The final sentence withholds coverage for "any loss arising from any act or omission by an Insured Person's estate, heirs, legal representatives, assigns, or spouse," which may take back the very coverage the subsection grants. Where the grant ends and the carve-out begins is unclear.

This coverage is deleted for the Brokerage/Advisory, Fiduciary and Securities Liability Insuring Agreements by paragraph 2.A of Endorsements 5091, 5093 and 5098. Whether any Not-for-Profit Directorship coverage survives across the Policy as a whole must be read from those endorsements.

The right to purchase is triggered by conversion only "subject to Section XIII (C)(1)(b)," but Section XIII (C)(2) says the occurrence of ANY of the conversion events in (C)(1) — including Financial Impairment under (C)(1)(a) — shall not affect the right to purchase the Discovery Period. The two provisions give different triggers.

The Discovery Period covers Wrongful Acts occurring before "the effective date of cancellation, nonrenewal or conversion," while the amended Section IV (E) in the Discovery Period Endorsement uses "prior to the termination date of this Policy" as its cut-off. Which date limits the covered Wrongful Acts is left unresolved.

The premium formula multiplies the Item 10(a) annual premium by the Item 4 percentage, but the Discovery Period Activation Endorsement instead sets out its own fixed premium figures per Insuring Agreement. Which controls if they diverge is not addressed.

The sixty-day lapse period runs from "the effective date of such cancellation, nonrenewal or conversion," but conversion under Section XIII (C) is an event with no stated effective date or notice. When the clock starts on a conversion is therefore uncertain.

The Discovery Period limit is made part of the immediately preceding Policy Year's Item 8 limit, yet the Discovery Period Activation Endorsement lists fresh per-Agreement limits ($10,000,000 D&O, $5,000,000 etc.) for the Discovery Period. Whether the Discovery Period has its own limits or shares the expiring year's is the conflict.

"Terms, conditions, Limits of Liability, retentions, or premiums different from those applicable to the expiring Policy" sets no ceiling, so any renewal offer however onerous defeats the Discovery Period right. The boundary of a qualifying "offer" is undefined.

"All applications, attachments and materials submitted to the Insurer" for this or any predecessor policy is unbounded, and it is not said what "materials" means or how far back "indirect renewal or replacement" reaches. That matters because Section XV makes those materials the basis of the Policy.

The definition sweeps in "economic advice, financial advice or investment advisory services" generally while carving out advice on "the FDIC-insured component of any deposit account," so the line between covered banking advice and excluded Brokerage/Advisory Services is indistinct. The same phrase drives the Section V (B) exclusion.

"A written or oral demand for monetary damages or non-monetary relief" has no threshold of formality, so whether a regulator's or receiver's demand letter or tolling request is a Claim (and when it was "first made") is open. The list is also confined to enumerated proceedings, which raises whether informal investigations qualify.

This definition is deleted and replaced by paragraph 4 of the Discovery Period Activation Endorsement, which substitutes a different definition including "the acquiring entity." Which definition of Company governs a Claim first made in the Discovery Period must be worked out between the two.

"Reasonable and necessary legal fees and expenses" is not measured against any benchmark, and Section IX (B)(2) leaves the Insurer to evaluate reasonableness and necessity itself. What is reasonable and necessary is a standing point of construction.

The statute is misnamed as the "Employment Retirement Income Security Act" rather than the Employee Retirement Income Security Act. The mistake is mechanical but the term drives both the ERISA Exclusion and the Fiduciary Liability Insuring Agreement.

The definition excludes "a Leased Employee or Independent Contractor," capitalized as defined terms though neither is defined anywhere in Section IV. Who is excluded from "Employee," and therefore from "Insured Person," is left undetermined.

"Financial Impairment" is defined as a status "of the Company" but the enumerated triggers include the appointment of a receiver over "the Company or any Subsidiary," so it is unclear whether a Subsidiary receivership impairs the Company. The definition is applied elsewhere (Section VII (B), the Discovery Endorsement) to entities other than the Company.

This definition of Insured is deleted and replaced for Fiduciary Liability purposes by paragraph 2.C of Endorsement 5093, which adds Employee Benefit Plans. Which definition applies to a Claim implicating more than one Insuring Agreement is not addressed.

"Insured Person" sweeps in every past, present or future Employee of the Company, which is far broader than the directors-and-officers cover the Policy is titled for. That breadth drives the reach of the Insured vs. Insured Exclusion in Section V (J), which bars Claims by "any Insured Person in any capacity."

"Common nexus [in] any fact, circumstance, situation, event, transaction or series of related facts" has no limiting principle, so almost any group of acts can be aggregated. Because Section VII (C) makes Interrelated Wrongful Acts a single Claim with one limit and one deemed date, the vagueness is consequential.

"Loss" excludes "any matters which are uninsurable under the law pursuant to which this Policy shall be construed" while expressly including punitive damages "where insurable by law," leaving the insurability question wholly undefined and no choice-of-law rule to answer it. Exclusion (7) for "restitution, disgorgement, or payment of similar sums" compounds the uncertainty over compensatory recoveries.

"The first named entity set forth of Item 1" depends on a list that is garbled in the original Declarations and reordered by the 2007 amendment, which puts Vantus Bank first. Who the Named Insured is at any given date therefore turns on which version of Item 1 is read.

"Or any earlier termination date" gives the Policy Period a moving end point that must be squared with the Amendment to Declarations extending expiry to 05/13/2009 and the Discovery Endorsement terminating the Policy on that date. The controlling end date is not fixed by this definition alone.

The definition says an extension is "part of the Policy Year which would have ended on the original expiration date," which must be applied to the one-month extension to 05/13/2009 made by the Amendment to Declarations. Whether Claims made in that month fall in the third Policy Year, and hence share its limit under Section VII (A)(2), is left to be worked out.

"Pollutants include but are not limited to" any "organism, irritant or contaminant," a non-exhaustive catch-all attached to a list of specifics with no outer boundary. The open-ended definition drives the whole of the Section V (K) exclusion.

The definition uses "more than fifty percent" for entities and joint ventures but "fifty percent (50%) or more" for limited liability companies, an inconsistency that decides control at exactly 50%. The text is also transposed, with subsection (1) printed before the defining words "Subsidiary means."

Subsection (5), "trustee exercising any other trust or fiduciary powers permitted by law," is a catch-all sitting against four enumerated categories, so its reach against the specifics is contestable. It governs the scope of the Section V (P) Trust Department Services Exclusion.

"While acting solely in the capacity as such" is the pivotal limit on a Wrongful Act and is nowhere elaborated, so mixed-capacity conduct by a director who is also an officer or shareholder falls outside any stated rule. The word "solely" invites a narrower reading than the Insuring Agreements assume.

This says the Section V Exclusions apply to all Insureds under all Insuring Agreements, but Endorsements 5091 and 5093 delete Exclusions (B) and (E) for their respective Insuring Agreements and 5098 adds others. The blanket statement cannot be given full effect alongside those endorsements.

The exclusion reaches "damage to or destruction of any tangible or intangible property," a phrase broad enough to capture ordinary economic loss claims that the Policy elsewhere insures. Where "intangible property" damage ends and covered financial loss begins is undefined.

This exclusion is deleted for the Brokerage/Advisory Services Insuring Agreement by paragraph 2.B of Endorsement 5091, while remaining applicable to every other Insuring Agreement. Whether a Claim touching Brokerage/Advisory Services is excluded from the D&O Agreements but covered under the endorsement is the resulting question.

"Totally without the solicitation, assistance, participation, or intervention of any Insured" sets an absolute standard with no de minimis line, so any cooperation by an insured defeats the security holder's Claim. The same formula appears in Section V (J)(3), which raises which one governs a derivative suit.

Subsection (3), "any other violation of any statutory or common law relating to employment," is a catch-all appended to two lists of specific employment wrongs and could swallow claims unrelated to the enumerated conduct. Its reach against the specifics is a classic ejusdem generis question.

This exclusion is deleted for the Fiduciary Liability Insuring Agreement by paragraph 2.D of Endorsement 5093, which then insures ERISA violations outright. Whether an ERISA-related Claim against directors under Insuring Agreement (A) is excluded while the same facts are covered under the Fiduciary endorsement is unresolved between the two.

The exclusion bars claims involving property "acquired by the Company as security or collateral for any loan," yet the carve-back restores Claims "in connection with the foreclosure process," and every foreclosed asset is acquired as collateral. Where the exclusion ends and the exception begins is unclear on the face of the clause.

The exclusion applies only "provided a final judgment or adjudication establishes" the fraudulent or criminal act, without saying whether the adjudication must be in the underlying action or may be in a coverage proceeding. That distinction decides whether the Insurer can invoke the exclusion at all.

The exclusion applies to Claims involving, "in fact," the gaining of profit or "conflicts of interest, engaging in self-dealing, or acting in bad faith," but says nothing about who establishes the fact or by what standard. Unlike Section V (G) it carries no final-adjudication requirement, so the trigger is undefined.

The parenthetical carve-out for "Insurance Services relating to credit life or disability insurance incidental to the issuance of a loan" turns on the undefined word "incidental." The same phrase appears in the definition of Brokerage/Advisory Services, so its scope has cross-cutting effect.

"Any Claim by, on behalf of, or at the behest of the Company" does not say whether a receiver, conservator or successor suing in the Company's right is the Company for this purpose, and the enumerated exceptions do not mention one. That is the central construction question the exclusion presents.

The exclusion must be read against the amended definition of Company in paragraph 4 of the Discovery Period Activation Endorsement, which makes "the acquiring entity" part of the Company. Whether a Claim by the acquirer or its assignee is thereby excluded is a conflict between the two provisions.

The exclusion extends to Claims "including Claims alleging damage to the Company or its security holders," which reaches shareholder suits over disclosure rather than pollution itself. Whether pure financial claims with a pollution backdrop are excluded is undetermined.

The exclusion bites on any fact or circumstance "which has been the subject of any notice given to any carrier other than the Insurer," with no requirement that the notice was accepted, valid, or given by an Insured. Its outer limit is undefined.

"Arising out of or in any way involving the same or substantially the same fact, circumstance or situation underlying" prior litigation has no stated degree of connection required. Read with Section IV (M) on Interrelated Wrongful Acts, the exclusion's reach beyond the prior suit itself is contestable.

The exclusion carves out Claims "except as provided in Section XII (C)(3)," but Section XII (C) contains only subsections (1) and (2), so the exception points to nothing. The Discovery Period Endorsement moreover deletes Section XII entirely.

The exclusion covers Trust Department Services as defined in Section IV (W), which includes IRA and Keogh trusteeships, while Section IV (X)(2) and Item 11 contemplate coverage for IRA/Keogh Claims outside a Trust Department. Whether IRA/Keogh work is excluded or insured turns on that boundary.

The heading limits these Exclusions to Insuring Agreement (C), but Endorsements 5091, 5093 and 5098 reproduce several of them as Section V exclusions applicable to all Insureds. Which Insuring Agreements a given exclusion reaches is not determinable from this sentence alone.

"Brought directly or indirectly by or for the benefit of any insurance carrier" is open-ended and could reach any Claim in which an insurer has a subrogated or economic interest. The phrase "regardless in whose name such Claim is actually made" removes any nominal-party limit.

The exclusion turns on whether "such liability would be imposed regardless of the existence of such contract or agreement," a counterfactual test with no stated method of application. Whether a claim is contractual or independent is the point of construction.

"Disputes over fees, commissions, or charges for the Company's services" is not confined to claims for the return of fees, so it may reach any claim in which fees feature. Section IV (N)(7) already excludes fee return from Loss, which sharpens the question of what this adds.

This bars any Claim "involving the Financial Impairment of the Company or any Subsidiary," while Section XVI (I) says Financial Impairment of the Insured shall not release the Insurer from its obligations and Section VIII (B)(3) says the same of payment priority. The three cannot comfortably stand together where the insured bank fails.
Subsection (3)'s "provider of like services" is a catch-all attached to enumerated internet roles with no stated limiting characteristic. Ordinary online banking could be argued into or out of it.

Subsection (6), "any other investment banking activity," is a general catch-all following five specific activities and has no defined outer boundary. Whether ordinary bank advisory work is captured turns on ejusdem generis.

The exclusion applies to credit "in excess of the legal lending limit of the Company" without identifying the governing regulatory measure or the point at which the limit is tested beyond "the time of its making." Aggregation and regulatory-definition questions are left open.
The exclusion turns on whether the person "physically appeared before the Insured," without saying who bears the burden or how appearance is proved. Its trigger is otherwise unqualified.

The exclusion covers Claims involving "the Company's function or activity as receiver," which is capable of being read either as the Company acting as receiver for others or as a Claim brought in a receivership of the Company itself. That difference is decisive where the insured bank is itself in receivership.

The Total Policy Limit caps all Insuring Agreements combined at Item 3's $10,000,000, while Item 8 sets separate limits totalling $35,000,000 and Section VIII (A)(1) says Insuring Agreement (A)'s limit is not eroded by Company coverage. How the aggregate cap and the non-erosion promise coexist is unresolved.

"The D&O Limit of Liability set forth in Item 8" names a limit that Item 8 does not label as such — Item 8 lists a separate limit for each Insuring Agreement. Which figure is the "D&O Limit" that all other Agreements are part of is ambiguous.

The single-highest-limit rule applies to Claims "against the Company" only, saying nothing about Claims against both the Company and Insured Persons under multiple Agreements. Its interaction with Section VII (A)(1)'s combined cap is left unstated.

The reinstatement is tied to IRA/Keogh Claims "pursuant to Section IV(X)(2)," which defines Wrongful Acts outside any Trust Department, while Item 11 and Section V (P) treat IRA/Keogh trusteeship as excluded Trust Department Services. Whether there is any coverage capable of being reinstated depends on reconciling these.

The retention waiver applies where the Company is "not permitted or required by law to advance Defense Costs or indemnify," but Section VII (B)(2) imposes the Insuring Agreement (B) retention wherever the Company is legally permitted, regardless of actual payment. Which subsection governs a Company that is permitted but insolvent and unable to pay is contested between them.

This makes the Insuring Agreement (B) retention apply unless non-indemnification is "solely by reason of" Financial Impairment, while paragraph 3 of the Discovery Period Endorsement states the same rule for an acquiring entity without the word "solely." The two versions of the same test differ in a way that decides who bears the retention.

The subsection first says retentions under multiple Insuring Agreements are summed, then says the total retention "shall in no event exceed the largest of such applicable retentions." Those two sentences give opposite answers for the same Claim.

Payment of covered Loss is deferred to "final disposition of the Claim," which sits awkwardly with the current-basis advancement duty in Section IX (B)(1) and Section XIV (B)(1)(b). What counts as final disposition, and whether settlement qualifies, is not defined.

Claims arising from Interrelated Wrongful Acts are deemed first made on the earliest date "regardless of whether such date is before or during the Policy Period," which can relate a Claim back out of coverage entirely. Read with Section IV (M)'s open-ended nexus test, the relation-back rule's reach is a live construction question.

The non-erosion promise is keyed to a limit being "a sublimit of the D&O Policy," a term used nowhere else and not defined in Section IV. Whether the Item 8 limits are sublimits or separate limits, and hence whether this protection operates at all, is undetermined.

Loss is deemed paid under Insuring Agreement (B) even where no indemnification is actually granted, which affects the non-erosion of Insuring Agreement (A) promised in Section VIII (A)(1) and the payment priority in Section VIII (B). Whether the deeming erodes limits that (A)(1) protects is not addressed.

The trigger is Loss which "in the Insurer's judgment could reasonably exceed" the Total Policy Limit, leaving the priority of payments to the Insurer's own assessment with no objective standard. What review, if any, that judgment is subject to is unstated.

This preserves the Insurer's payment obligations notwithstanding Financial Impairment, while the Insolvency Exclusion in Section VI (D)(1) bars Loss on any Claim involving Financial Impairment of the Company. The two provisions point in opposite directions when the insured fails.

The Insured "shall only retain counsel that is mutually agreed upon with the Insurer," which qualifies the same paragraph's statement that defence is the Insured's own duty. What follows if agreement is never reached, on a no-duty-to-defend policy, is not addressed.

The Insured may not "incur Defense Costs" at all without the Insurer's prior written consent, which sits uneasily with the Insured's own duty to defend in Section IX (A)(1) and the advancement obligation in Section IX (B)(1). Whether consent must precede every step of the defence is the point of conflict.

The Insurer's right "to effectively associate" in defence and settlement is undefined beyond a non-exhaustive list, on a policy that disclaims any duty to defend. How far association may go before it becomes control is left open.

Advancement is owed "on a current basis" but is expressly "Subject to Section XIV," under which the Insurer advances only Defense Costs "which the Insurer believes to be covered." The extent of the advancement duty differs between the two provisions.

Notice must be given "as soon as practicable" but "in no event later than sixty (60) days," two different standards for the same condition precedent. Whether notice within sixty days can still be late for not being as soon as practicable is the ambiguity.

The notice of circumstances must "contain full particulars" including the identity of potential plaintiffs and the causes of action to be asserted, a standard that may be impossible to satisfy before a Claim exists. What suffices as full particulars, on a condition precedent, is undefined.

The sentence is garbled where the verb should be ("under this Policy 9.. given to the Insurer"), so it is unclear whether notice at the Item 5 address is mandatory or merely permitted. Section XIII (B)(1) meanwhile requires notice to the Named Insured at the Item 1 address.

Cooperation "as the Insurer may reasonably request" is made a condition precedent to coverage without any limit as to privileged or work-product material. The boundary of a reasonable request is the point of construction.

This subsection is deleted and replaced by Endorsement 2223, which substitutes a 20% asset threshold for the 25% stated here, and is then deleted in its entirety by the Discovery Period Activation Endorsement. Which version, if any, governs a transaction is not determinable from this text.

The automatic coverage threshold of "less than twenty-five percent (25%)" is replaced with 20% by Endorsement 2223, leaving acquisitions between 20% and 25% of assets treated oppositely under the two texts. Section IV (E) also makes bank Subsidiary coverage "subject to Section XII (B)."

Endorsement 2223 replaces only Section XII (A) and (B) and says "all other provisions of Section XII shall remain unchanged," while the Discovery Period Endorsement deletes Section XII in its entirety. Whether subsection (C) survives into the Discovery Period is the conflict.

The Insurer returns only 90% of unearned premium on the Named Insured's cancellation, whereas Section XIII (C)(2) says that after a conversion event the Policy "may not be cancelled" and the premium is fully earned. Whether a Named Insured can cancel at all after conversion is unresolved between the two.

This subsection is deleted and replaced by the Iowa Amendatory Endorsement 8790D, which permits cancellation only on enumerated statutory grounds. Which notice regime governs an actual cancellation must be settled between them.

The Insurer must return 100% of unearned premium on its own cancellation, while Section III and the Discovery Period Endorsement make the Discovery Period premium fully earned and noncancellable. The two rules collide if the Insurer cancels during the Discovery Period.

"The Company ceasing to engage actively in its primary business" is undefined and has no measure of degree or time, yet it converts the Policy to run-off. "Primary business" is also unidentified for a group of eight named insured entities.

This preserves the right to purchase the Discovery Period on the occurrence of "any of the foregoing events," while Section III makes conversion a trigger only "subject to Section XIII (C)(1)(b)." The two provisions differ over whether Financial Impairment under (C)(1)(a) confers that right.

Conversion for a Subsidiary comprising "less than fifty percent" of assets is addressed here and for one comprising "more than fifty percent" in (C)(1)(a), so a Subsidiary at exactly fifty percent falls in neither. The gap is on the face of the two subsections read together.

This treats 100% of jointly incurred Loss as Loss of the Insured Persons, while Section XIV (A)(2) requires allocation between covered and uncovered Loss by relative legal exposure. Which rule applies to a Claim that is both joint and partly uncovered is unresolved.

Allocation "based on the relative legal exposures of the parties" supplies no method, no decision-maker and no time at which exposure is measured. The phrase is the operative standard for every disputed allocation.

The subsection allocates by "relative legal exposures" while Section XIV (A)(1)(a) assigns 100% of jointly incurred Loss to the Insured Persons without allocation. The two allocation rules give different answers on the same Claim.

The Insurer advances only those Defense Costs "which the Insurer believes to be covered," a subjective test that qualifies the unconditional advancement duty in Section IX (B)(1). Where the Insurer believes nothing is covered, the obligation may be empty.

Binding arbitration is available only "if requested by the Insured" and only for "the allocation dispute," leaving all other coverage disputes and any Insurer-initiated reference outside the clause. The boundary of an arbitrable allocation dispute is undefined.

Retroactive reallocation "applied retroactively to all Defense Costs" implies a right of recoupment of amounts already advanced, but the clause says nothing about repayment, unlike the express repayment promise in Section IX (B)(1). Whether recoupment follows is left to construction.

The Application is to be "construed as a separate Application for coverage by each Insured Person," which points toward severability, while subsection (2) of the same clause denies that the Policy is a series of individual contracts. Whether an innocent director's coverage is severable turns on this tension.

Denying that the Policy is "a series of individual insurance contracts" cannot easily be squared with subsection (1)'s separate-Application rule and Section XV (C)(1)'s non-imputation of knowledge among Insured Persons. The three together leave severability of the Application unsettled.

The statements in the Application are declared material and the Policy issued in reliance on them, without stating the consequence — rescission, avoidance, or the limited denial of coverage set out in the Severability clause. The remedy for a false statement is left to be inferred.

Subsections (1) to (3) withhold coverage only from those who "knew" of the undisclosed fact, but the closing sentence says the conditions apply "whether or not the Insured Person actually knew" of the misrepresentation. The clause contradicts itself on the knowledge requirement.

Knowledge is not imputed among Insured Persons for exclusion purposes, while Section XV (B) denies coverage to the Company by reference to senior officers' knowledge and Section XV (A)(2) denies the Policy is a series of individual contracts. The extent of severability across the instrument is unsettled.

Imputation to the Company is confined to "Section V, Exclusions (G) and (H)," so the treatment of officer knowledge under every other exclusion is unaddressed — an expressio unius question. "Any person holding any equivalent position (regardless of title)" also has no defined boundary.

Subrogation is to "all the Insured Persons' and the Company's rights to recovery," without any waiver against insureds, so the Insurer may on its face be subrogated to claims against its own insureds. The clause's limits are not stated.

The integration clause names "this Policy, the Application, and any written Endorsements," whereas the Declarations signature page says the Declarations, Application, Policy and Endorsements together constitute the contract. Which set of documents is integrated is different in the two statements.

Terms "in conflict with the terms of any applicable laws governing this Policy" are deemed amended, without identifying the applicable law or how the amendment is to read. The clause supplies no choice-of-law rule for a Policy issued to Iowa insureds by an Ohio insurer.

The Named Insured acts for all Insureds "for all purposes," but Section IV (P) defines the Named Insured by reference to Item 1, which the 2007 amendment reordered to put Vantus Bank first. Who holds that authority, and what becomes of it if that entity fails, is unresolved between the provisions.

No term may be waived or changed "except by written Endorsement," which must be read against the many Endorsements that themselves recite that nothing therein varies the Policy. Whether conduct or correspondence can ever modify coverage is the question.

No action lies unless there has been "full compliance with all the terms of this Policy" and the Insured's obligation to pay is finally determined by adjudication or by written agreement of Insureds, claimant AND Insurer. Whether this bars a declaratory coverage action before judgment is a live question.

The bar on joining the Insurer applies to "any Claim against the Insured," a defined term that includes coverage-related proceedings only indirectly. Whether a direct action by a claimant or receiver is precluded is not stated.

The Policy is made excess to "any other existing insurance regardless of whether collectable," which could reduce it to nothing where other cover exists on paper but is worthless. It also says the Policy "shall not be subject to the terms of any other insurance" while simultaneously subordinating itself to that insurance.

This says Financial Impairment of the Insured shall not release the Insurer from its obligations, while the Insolvency Exclusions in Section VI (D)(1) and in Endorsements 5091 and 5098 bar Loss on any Claim involving Financial Impairment of the Company. The two cannot both be given effect in a receivership.

This provision is deleted and replaced in identical terms, plus an extra paragraph, by paragraph 3 of the Securities Liability Endorsement 5098. Which version governs, and whether the added exclusivity paragraph applies policy-wide, must be resolved between them.

Headings "form no part of the terms and conditions of coverage," yet several operative provisions identify what they amend by heading — for example Section VI's title and the endorsements deleting Section II (B) "entitled 'Not-for-Profit Directorships'." The disclaimer cannot be applied literally without unsettling those cross-references.

The exclusion is added to Section V for all Insuring Agreements but is disapplied "to the Securities Liability Insuring Agreement, Form 5098," while Item 6 of the Declarations states that Insuring Agreement (C) includes Securities Liability coverage. Whether securities claims survive under (C) is a conflict between this exclusion and Item 6.
The clause preserves all Policy terms although the same Endorsement adds an entirely new exclusion to Section V. The scope of "other than as above stated" is the point of construction.

Coverage is stated to be "subject to all of the terms, conditions and limitations of this Endorsement," whereas paragraph 2 makes the Policy's terms apply except as listed. Whether the Endorsement or the Policy controls an unlisted conflict is not settled.

The Insuring Agreement pays on behalf of "the Insured," which includes the Company, but Section IV (X)(3) defines a Wrongful Act of the Company only "to the extent that coverage is granted to the Company by Insuring Agreement." Whether Company-level Brokerage/Advisory claims are covered depends on reading the two together.

This exclusion for disputes over "fees, commissions, or charges for the Company's services" is added to an endorsement whose whole subject is fee-earning brokerage and advisory work. How much of the granted coverage it takes back is unclear.

The proviso restores coverage where the Claim alleges a Wrongful Act "solely in connection with an Insured's investment on behalf of a customer" in stock of entities in items (2) and (3), leaving item (1) — Financial Impairment of the Company — without any carve-back. Whether the proviso can be read across all three items is the question.

The introductory words end without punctuation before the list ("involving the Company providing (1)..."), and subsection (3) closes with the catch-all "provider of like services." The reach of that catch-all beyond the enumerated internet roles is undefined.

Subsection (6)'s "any other investment banking activity" is a catch-all following five specific activities, with no stated limiting principle. Its scope against the enumerated specifics is contestable.

The exclusion reaches "actual or written representations, promises or guarantees" — the word "actual" plainly standing where "oral" belongs. Whether oral representations are excluded turns on that mechanical error.

"Mechanical or electronic failure, breakdown or malfunction of any machine or system of machines" is broad enough to capture computer and trading-system errors underlying ordinary advisory claims. Its boundary against the coverage granted is undefined.

"The Company's function or activity as receiver, trustee in bankruptcy, or assignee" can be read as the Company acting in those roles for others or as claims arising in a receivership of the Company itself. That ambiguity is decisive where the insured institution fails.
The clause reads "arising out or in any way involving," omitting the word "of" from the standard formula. The mechanical slip leaves the causal connective incomplete.
The preservation sentence appears in an Endorsement that deletes Section II (B) and Exclusion (B) and adds nine new exclusions. What it preserves beyond "as above stated" is arguable.
Coverage is made subject to the terms of "this Endorsement," while paragraph 2 applies the Policy's terms except as listed. Which prevails on an unlisted conflict is unaddressed.

The Insuring Agreement covers "Wrongful Acts resulting from the Administration of any Employee Benefit Plan," but Section IV (X) defines Wrongful Act only by reference to Insured Persons acting in their capacity as such, IRA/Keogh trusteeships and the Company — and this Endorsement does not amend that definition. Whether plan-administration conduct is a Wrongful Act at all must be settled between the two.

"Administration" is confined to counselling, interpreting, record-handling and enrolment, which is narrower than the fiduciary duties ERISA imposes and which the Insuring Agreement separately insures. The relationship between the narrow definition and the broader ERISA limb of the grant is unclear.

The plan must be "operated solely by the Company or jointly by the Company and a labor organization," which excludes plans run with a third-party administrator or a predecessor employer. The word "solely" leaves plans jointly administered with anyone else outside the definition.
Subsection (1) is garbled ("medical, 4 or hospital care or benefits"), so one of the enumerated benefit types cannot be read. The list is closed by "including," leaving its exhaustiveness uncertain.

The definition brings in Employee Benefit Plans acquired "pursuant to Section XII," a Section that Endorsement 2223 partly replaced and the Discovery Period Activation Endorsement deleted in its entirety. Whether the acquisition limb has any content is a conflict with those endorsements.

Exclusion (2) removes "criminal or civil fines or penalties imposed by law" from Loss, while the closing sentence says Loss shall not exclude the 5% and 20% civil penalties under ERISA sections 502(i) and (l). The provision states and then unstates the same exclusion.

This replaces Section V (J) for Fiduciary purposes by adding a fourth carve-out, so the Insured vs. Insured Exclusion has two different texts in the same Policy. Which text applies to a Claim implicating both fiduciary and D&O coverage is unresolved.

The exclusion repeatedly refers to an "other Employee Program," a term used nowhere else and defined nowhere in the Policy or the Endorsement. What plans beyond a defined Employee Benefit Plan it captures is undetermined.

This Insolvency Exclusion omits the Financial Impairment limb that the corresponding exclusions in Section VI (D) and Endorsements 5091 and 5098 contain. Whether a fiduciary Claim involving the Company's own Financial Impairment is excluded depends on comparing the versions.

The exclusion bars Claims involving duties imposed by COBRA and other employment statutes, while the Fiduciary Insuring Agreement covers violations of duties relating to any Employee Benefit Plan, which include COBRA continuation obligations. The grant and the exclusion overlap on the same facts.

This adds a reinstatement of "the Limit of Liability under this Endorsement," but Item 3's Total Policy Limit caps all Insuring Agreements combined and Section VII (A)(1) says so "regardless" of sublimits. Whether a reinstated fiduciary limit can exceed the Total Policy Limit is unresolved between them.
The clause preserves the Policy's terms although the Endorsement redefines Insured and Loss and rewrites Exclusion (J). The scope of "other than as above stated" is the construction point.
Coverage is made subject to the terms of "this Endorsement" while paragraph 2 applies the Policy's terms save as listed. Which governs an unlisted conflict is not stated.

The Agreement pays on behalf of "the Insured," including the Company, for Wrongful Acts connected with securities the Company issued, while Item 6 of the Declarations says Insuring Agreement (C) already includes Securities Liability coverage and Endorsement 2949 excludes securities claims elsewhere. Which Agreement responds to a securities Claim must be resolved across those provisions.

Unlike the corresponding exclusion in Endorsement 5091, this version carries no proviso preserving claims involving customer investments, though the two are otherwise identical. Whether the omission is deliberate is a question raised by reading the endorsements together.

Subsection (6), "any other investment banking activity," is a catch-all appended to five enumerated activities in an endorsement that insures securities claims. Its scope against the specifics is a general-versus-specific question.

"The Company's function or activity as receiver, trustee in bankruptcy, or assignee for the benefit of creditors" can be read either as the Company acting in those roles or as a Claim arising out of a receivership of the Company. The difference matters where a receiver of the insured brings the Claim.

This reproduces Section XVI (J) verbatim while purporting to delete and replace it, so the same anti-stacking rule appears twice in the instrument with only the added exclusivity paragraph to distinguish them. Which text governs a Claim outside the Securities Endorsement is unclear.

Making Securities Liability coverage exclusive of "any other Insuring Agreement" cannot be squared with Section VII (A)(3), which contemplates a Claim subject to more than one Insuring Agreement, or with Item 6's statement that Insuring Agreement (C) includes Securities Liability coverage. It also cuts across the non-erosion protection for Insuring Agreement (A) in Section VIII (A)(1).
The preservation sentence sits in an Endorsement that deletes and replaces Section XVI (J) and adds exclusions. What survives "as above stated" is the construction point.

This replaces Section XII (A) with a 20% asset threshold in place of 25%, and is itself deleted along with the whole of Section XII by the Discovery Period Activation Endorsement. Which threshold, if any, applied to a given transaction is unresolved across the three texts.

Automatic coverage is given for banks below 20% of assets, whereas the unamended Section XII (B) — to which the definition of Company in Section IV (E) is expressly "subject" — uses 25%. Acquisitions falling between the two thresholds are treated oppositely.
The clause preserves the Policy's terms although the same Endorsement deletes and replaces Section XII (A) and (B). The scope of "other than as above stated" is arguable.

The disclosure states that terrorism coverage is included yet that the premium attributable to it is "$0.00," which is internally odd for a purported priced coverage. Whether the notice creates or merely describes coverage is not stated.

Subsection (c) introduces six lettered cancellation grounds but the enumeration is broken, printing only "i. 1. iil. iv." detached from the reasons that follow. Which reason bears which number, and whether all six are within subsection (c), cannot be read off the text.
The clause preserves the Policy's terms although the Endorsement deletes and replaces Section XIII (B)(1). What "other than as above stated" leaves standing is the construction point.
